my_independent_answer: State-based actions (SBAs) are checked every time a player would receive priority, per 704.3: right before priority would be given, SBAs are checked and all applicable ones performed simultaneously as one event; if any were performed, repeat; if none were performed, waiting triggered abilities go on the stack and the check repeats again; only when a check does nothing and nothing is waiting does the player actually get priority. The same loop runs during cleanup (514), except if the first check there does nothing and nothing triggers, no one gets priority and the step just ends.
answer_note: Matches 704.3 verbatim in substance; cleanup-step exception correctly stated.
question_note: Unambiguous, tests real procedural knowledge (the SBA/trigger interleaving loop), not trivial.
cr_evidence: 704.3: Whenever a player would get priority... the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event... This process also occurs during the cleanup step... except that if no state-based actions are performed as the result of the step's first check and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, then no player gets priority and the step ends.

my_independent_answer: A player can concede at any time, in any game, for any reason (104.3a); conceding is an immediate loss. Even a player under another player's control (e.g. via a control-another-player effect) retains the right to concede whenever they want -- the controller cannot force or block a concession (723.6).
answer_note: Matches 104.3a and 723.6 exactly; correctly notes the controlled-player carve-out.
question_note: Clear, single correct answer with a non-obvious edge case (controlled players) that adds discriminating value.
cr_evidence: 104.3a: A player can concede the game at any time... 723.6: The controller of another player can't make that player concede. A player may concede the game at any time, even if they are controlled by another player.

my_independent_answer: The active player is whoever's turn it currently is (102.1); nonactive players are everyone else. No calculation needed, just look at whose turn is in progress.
answer_note: Matches 102.1 and the glossary entry exactly.
question_note: Single-sentence tautological definition (active player = whose turn it is) with no edge cases, exceptions, or reasoning required; unlikely to discriminate a good rules-bot from a bad one.
cr_evidence: 102.1: The active player is the player whose turn it is. The other players are nonactive players. Glossary "Active Player": The player whose turn it is. See rule 102.1.

my_independent_answer: The nonactive player who cast the spell gets priority back first. 117.3c applies to any player regardless of active/nonactive status: whoever had priority and used it to cast a spell/activate an ability/take a special action gets priority again afterward (after the 117.5 SBA/trigger check).
answer_note: Correctly generic application of 117.3c; correctly notes the SBA/trigger check via 117.5 happens first.
question_note: Tests whether the system knows priority-after-casting isn't restricted to the active player (a real potential confusion point with 117.3a/117.3b, which are worded around the active player). See q026/q027 redundancy note below.
cr_evidence: 117.3c: If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward.

my_independent_answer: The active player gets priority back first, since 117.3c doesn't distinguish active from nonactive -- whoever cast the spell (while holding priority) gets priority again afterward.

The pair tests two different failure modes even though the ground-truth rule is identical, so I would not drop either purely for redundancy -- though if the eval set needs trimming, this pair is the most defensible place to cut one.

my_independent_answer: Lore counters go on a Saga at two distinct trigger points, not one: (1) as it enters the battlefield -- via 714.3a's replacement effect (exactly 1 counter) for Sagas WITHOUT read ahead, OR via 714.3b's replacement effect (a chosen number between 1 and the final chapter number) for Sagas WITH read ahead -- and (2) as a turn-based action under 714.3c, at the start of the controller's precombat main phase, one counter added to each Saga they control with a chapter ability, not using the stack. I independently confirmed 714.3b is a real, separate replacement effect (cross-referenced by 702.155b) and is not merely a variant wording of 714.3a -- it applies only to read-ahead Sagas and produces a different (chosen, possibly >1) counter count on entry.

my_independent_answer: A delayed triggered ability is a triggered ability created by an effect (typically during resolution of a spell/ability, or when a replacement effect applies) that fires later at some future event rather than acting immediately. It contains 'when'/'whenever'/'at' but that word usually isn't first in the ability text (603.7).
answer_note: Matches 603.7 and the glossary entry exactly.
question_note: Requires distinguishing this from an ordinary triggered ability (created by an effect rather than existing on an object), so not purely rote.
cr_evidence: 603.7: An effect may create a delayed triggered ability that can do something at a later time. Glossary: An ability created by effects generated when some spells or abilities resolve, or when some replacement effects are applied, that does something later on rather than at that time.

my_independent_answer: Yes. Instants/sorceries primarily have spell abilities (113.3a: any text on an instant/sorcery is a spell ability unless it's an activated, triggered, or static ability fitting 113.6's exceptions). So a non-permanent spell CAN carry activated/triggered/static abilities in the specific cases 113.6 lists (e.g. 113.6e ability restricting how it can be cast, 113.6g can't-be-countered ability), even though normally abilities of instants/sorceries function only on the stack (113.6's general rule) rather than persisting off-stack the way permanent abilities do.
answer_note: Correct and matches 113.3a and 113.6 framing precisely.

my_independent_answer: Yes. Split second (702.61a) only blocks casting other spells or activating non-mana abilities while the split-second spell is on the stack. 702.61b explicitly carves out mana abilities and special actions as still allowed, and says triggered abilities still trigger and go on the stack normally.
question_note: Clear, tests a specific carve-out (mana abilities vs. other abilities) that's a common source of confusion, so not trivial.
cr_evidence: 702.61a: 'Split second' means 'As long as this spell is on the stack, players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities.' 702.61b: Players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack.
